main.title: Siren
main.subtitle: A village seen through frightened eyes
main.summary: Siren is Sony's PlayStation 2 survival-horror game, first released in Japan on 6 November 2003. Several characters become trapped in Hanuda, a village inhabited by hostile shibito, with their experiences unfolding across an interwoven chronology. The player can borrow another person's or creature's sight, gathering information from a position the controlled character may not safely reach. The ability makes seeing an active part of survival. A route through the village depends on understanding where a threat is looking and what its view reveals about a place that remains dangerous to explore directly.

cards.heading: A village seen through frightened eyes
cards.text: Siren is Sony's PlayStation 2 survival-horror game, first released in Japan on 6 November 2003. Several characters become trapped in Hanuda, a village inhabited by hostile shibito, with their experiences unfolding across an interwoven chronology. The player can borrow another person's or creature's sight, gathering information from a position the controlled character may not safely reach. The ability makes seeing an active part of survival. A route through the village depends on understanding where a threat is looking and what its view reveals about a place that remains dangerous to explore directly.

cards.heading: Watch the patrol without standing in front of it
cards.text: Sightjacking allows the player to study an enemy's surroundings and movements while the protagonist remains elsewhere. The information can reveal when a path becomes safer or where a useful object lies. It does not remove the risk of acting on that knowledge, because returning to the controlled character means leaving the borrowed viewpoint behind. Objectives connect the cast's separate scenarios, giving one person's action consequences for another part of the story. Progress involves learning both the village and the relationships between events, making attention to another perspective useful in more than one way.

cards.heading: A horror director builds another unsettling place
cards.text: Keiichiro Toyama directed and co-wrote the game after his work on the original Silent Hill, with Naoko Sato contributing to the writing and Hitomi Shimizu composing the music. The European and Australian release used the title Forbidden Siren in March 2004, with North America following in April. Reviews praised the atmosphere and originality while finding the play demanding and sometimes obscure. A sequel and later reimagining continued the world. The original's distinctive fear lies in knowing that seeing through an enemy can help the player survive, while also bringing that enemy's presence uncomfortably close.

main.title: Mario Kart: Double Dash
main.summary: Two riders share each kart in Mario Kart: Double Dash!!. The GameCube racer builds new tactics around its paired characters while taking the Mario cast across sixteen themed tracks.

cards.heading: Mario Kart: Double Dash
cards.text: Mario Kart: Double Dash!! is a 2003 kart racing game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It is the fourth main entry in the Mario Kart series. Similar to previous titles, Double Dash challenges Mario series player characters to race against each other on 16 Mario-themed tracks. The game introduced a number of gameplay features, such as having two riders per kart.

cards.heading: Two riders find a GameCube audience
cards.text: Double Dash released in November 2003 and received positive reviews from critics, who praised the graphics, new gameplay features, character and item rosters, arcade aesthetic and track design, but the audio received mixed reactions. It was commercially successful, with more than 3.8 million copies sold in the United States, and more than 802,000 copies sold in Japan. It is the second best-selling GameCube game of all-time, selling around 7 million copies worldwide, behind Super Smash Bros. Melee.

main.title: Mario Party 5
main.subtitle: A party inside the Dream Depot
main.summary: Mario Party 5 is Hudson Soft's second GameCube party game, first released in North America on 11 November 2003.

cards.heading: A party inside the Dream Depot
cards.text: Mario Party 5 is Hudson Soft's second GameCube party game, first released in North America on 11 November 2003. The Dream Depot provides a set of fantastical boards where Mario and the other players compete for Stars. Coins earned through movement and minigames help shape that contest, while a single-player story pits the chosen character against Bowser's Koopa Kids. The setting gives each board another playful theme, but the larger rhythm remains a gathering repeatedly interrupted by small tests of reactions, cooperation and luck.

cards.heading: Leave an effect for the next traveler
cards.text: Capsules introduce a different item system. They can affect a player directly or be placed on board spaces, leaving an effect for whoever later reaches them. Extra movement, stolen coins and other changes make the route a place the competitors can modify as well as traverse. A player must consider both the immediate benefit of an item and what it might do to someone else's next turn. Minigames continue to replenish the coins that keep those small acts of interference possible.

cards.heading: Build another kind of rivalry
cards.text: Super Duel adds a separate activity in which players assemble battle vehicles from parts and fight other machines. It extends the competitive gathering beyond the boards, offering a more direct contest around a personally built vehicle. Toad, Boo and Koopa Kid join the playable roster, and Aya Tanaka composed the music. Mario Party 5 uses the Dream Depot's variety to connect several scales of competition: a whole board match, a minigame lasting moments and a vehicle battle whose outcome depends on the machine brought into it.

main.title: Ratchet & Clank: Going Commando
main.summary: Weapons grow through use as Ratchet and Clank follow a stolen experiment across the Bogon galaxy.

cards.heading: The game
cards.text: Ratchet & Clank: Going Commando is Insomniac Games' 2003 PlayStation 2 shooter-platformer, released in much of Europe as Ratchet & Clank 2: Locked & Loaded. The sequel sends the partners to the Bogon galaxy, where Megacorp hires Ratchet to recover a stolen experiment. New equipment and weapon development accompany the journey between planets.

cards.heading: An arsenal with different jobs
cards.text: The starting Lancer fires a rapid stream of shots, while the Gravity Bomb gives an explosion a place in the same encounter. Later equipment adds other shapes of attack: the Chopper sends bouncing discs, and the Mini-Turret Glove places a weapon that can keep firing while Ratchet moves. Those differences make a purchase more than another damage number. A crowded platform, a moving target and an approach from several sides give the player reasons to change the tool in hand.

cards.heading: Keep using it, watch it change
cards.text: Many of the new weapons gain experience through use and transform when their bar fills. The Lancer becomes the Heavy Lancer; the Gravity Bomb becomes the Mini-Nuke. Choosing a familiar favourite therefore competes with bringing another weapon towards its upgrade. Ratchet's own Nanotech capacity also grows through combat, increasing the punishment he can survive. Bolts buy equipment and supplies, tying the spectacle of scattered machinery to the next practical decision at a vendor: ammunition now, or money saved for another weapon.

cards.heading: A race between the battles
cards.text: Hoverbike races interrupt the planetary firefights with circuits built around speed, steering and attacks on competing riders. A race asks the player to read the route ahead while watching rivals close enough to interfere. Other parts of the adventure return to Clank's smaller scale, gadgets and platforming routes, giving the pair different ways through an obstacle. Moving between those activities keeps the next destination varied: a planet may offer a fight, a new piece of equipment or a competition worth returning to.

main.title: Beyond Good & Evil
main.summary: Beyond Good & Evil is a 2003 action-adventure game developed by Ubisoft Montpellier and published by Ubisoft for PlayStation 2, Windows, Xbox, and GameCube.

cards.text: Beyond Good & Evil is a 2003 action-adventure game developed by Ubisoft Montpellier and published by Ubisoft for PlayStation 2, Windows, Xbox, and GameCube. The story follows the adventures of Jade, an investigative reporter, martial artist, and spy working with a resistance movement to reveal a sinister alien conspiracy. Players control Jade and other allies, solving puzzles, fighting enemies, obtaining photographic evidence and, later in the game, travelling to space.

Michel Ancel, creator of the Rayman series, envisioned the game as the first part of a trilogy. The game was developed under the codename "Project BG&E" by 30 employees of Ubisoft's studio divisions in Montpellier and Milan, with production lasting more than three years. One of the main goals of the game is to create a meaningful story while giving players much freedom, though the game adopts a relatively linear structure. The game was received poorly when it was shown at E3 2002, and it prompted the developers to change some of the game's elements, including Jade's design. Ancel also attempted to streamline the game in order to make it more commercially appealing.

Beyond Good & Evil received generally favorable reviews upon release, with critics praising the game's animation, setting, story and design, but criticizing its combat and technical issues. The game received a nomination for "Game of the Year" at the 2004 Game Developers Choice Awards. While the game was considered a commercial failure at launch, it has since developed a cult following and is even considered by some to be one of the greatest video games ever made.

A full HD remastered version of the game was released on Xbox Live Arcade and PlayStation Network in 2011. Another remaster, titled the 20th Anniversary Edition, was released in 2024. A sequel, Beyond Good and Evil 2, was announced in 2008.

main.title: Need for Speed: Underground
main.summary: Need for Speed: Underground is a 2003 racing video game and the seventh installment in the Need for Speed series following Hot Pursuit 2 (2002).

cards.heading: EA Black Box takes Underground
cards.text: Need for Speed: Underground is a 2003 racing video game and the seventh installment in the Need for Speed series following Hot Pursuit 2 (2002). It was developed by EA Black Box and published by Electronic Arts. Versions were produced for consoles and Microsoft Windows, with a separate adaptation for the Game Boy Advance. An arcade version developed and published by Global VR came out two years later.

cards.heading: Custom cars in Olympic City
cards.text: Unlike previous Need for Speed games, which featured sports cars and exotics, Underground featured vehicles associated with the import scene. It was the first game in the series to offer a career mode that features a comprehensive storyline, and a garage mode that allowed players to fully customize their cars with a large variety of brand-name performance and visual upgrades. All races take place in Olympic City, a fictional setting drawing on Vancouver, Los Angeles, San Francisco, New York City, London, and Paris.

cards.heading: A successful new direction
cards.text: Underground was critically and commercially successful, selling around 15 million units and receiving positive reviews. It was followed by Need for Speed: Underground 2 in 2004.

main.title: Manhunt
main.summary: Manhunt is a 2003 psychological horror stealth game developed by Rockstar North and published by Rockstar Games.

cards.heading: Stealth under the camera's gaze
cards.text: Manhunt is a 2003 psychological horror stealth game developed by Rockstar North and published by Rockstar Games. It was released for the PlayStation 2 in November 2003, followed by Microsoft Windows and Xbox releases in April 2004. Set within the fictional Carcer City, players control a death row inmate named James Earl Cash, who is forced to participate in a series of snuff films by killing criminal gang members sent to hunt him on camera.

cards.heading: A violent game and its contested reception
cards.text: The game received positive reviews from critics, with praise towards its dark tone and violent gameplay, although the combat and level design were criticized. Due to its graphic violence, Manhunt was the subject of significant controversy and banned in several countries. It was also implicated in a murder by the UK media, although this accusation was later rejected by the police and courts. While not a commercial hit, Manhunt developed a substantial cult following and was followed by a stand-alone sequel, Manhunt 2, in 2007. The PlayStation 2 version of the game was re-released through the PlayStation Network for the PlayStation 3 in 2013 and PlayStation 4 in 2016, and the Xbox version was re-released in 2021 through the Xbox Backwards Compatibility program.

main.title: Pokémon Colosseum
main.subtitle: Genius Sonority · GameCube
main.summary: Pokémon Colosseum is Genius Sonority's GameCube role-playing adventure set in the desert region of Orre. Wes, a former member of Team Snagem, travels with Rui to rescue Shadow Pokémon whose hearts have been closed by the organisation Cipher. These creatures are captured from opposing trainers rather than found through ordinary wild encounters. The premise gives the familiar act of throwing a Poké Ball another purpose. Acquiring a new companion begins with recognising that something has been done to it, then taking responsibility for helping it recover.

cards.heading: Rescue a Pokémon from the opposing trainer
cards.text: Pokémon Colosseum is Genius Sonority's GameCube role-playing adventure set in the desert region of Orre. Wes, a former member of Team Snagem, travels with Rui to rescue Shadow Pokémon whose hearts have been closed by the organisation Cipher. These creatures are captured from opposing trainers rather than found through ordinary wild encounters. The premise gives the familiar act of throwing a Poké Ball another purpose. Acquiring a new companion begins with recognising that something has been done to it, then taking responsibility for helping it recover.

cards.heading: Two partners stand together in battle
cards.text: Most encounters use Double Battles, putting two Pokémon on each side of the field. The player has to consider how the pair's moves and vulnerabilities work together, while keeping the targeted Shadow Pokémon alive long enough to capture it. Rui identifies the creatures that need rescuing. Purification then makes their recovery part of the longer journey rather than the end of a single fight. The party develops through both kinds of work: winning the next encounter and caring for the unusual new member brought out of it.

cards.heading: A complete journey beside the television
cards.text: Towns, colosseums and hostile bases connect the battles into an adventure with its own protagonist and supporting cast. Tsukasa Tawada's music gives Orre a distinctive sound alongside the much larger presentation of familiar Pokémon. Game Boy Advance connectivity allows trading and further battles with the handheld games. Released in Japan in 2003, Colosseum gave the home console more than another arena for a collection built elsewhere. Its rescue story established a separate place in which a new team could be assembled and developed through the player's own journey.

main.title: Gotcha Force
main.subtitle: A toy collection becomes a fighting force
main.summary: Gotcha Force is Capcom's arena action game, first released for GameCube in Japan on 27 November 2003.

cards.heading: A toy collection becomes a fighting force
cards.text: Gotcha Force is Capcom's arena action game, first released for GameCube in Japan on 27 November 2003. Children command teams of miniature Gotcha Borgs, collectible fighters whose different weapons and abilities turn small everyday environments into battlegrounds. The story follows Kou and his allies against the Death Force. Collecting and fighting are closely linked: a newly obtained Borg changes the possible lineup, while another match gives the player a chance to discover how that fighter behaves when placed against a moving opponent.

cards.heading: Each small fighter spends part of the budget
cards.text: Before a battle, the commander builds a force within a GF Energy allowance. More powerful Borgs consume more of that budget, creating a choice between a few expensive fighters and a larger sequence of cheaper ones. In the arena, lock-on targeting keeps the opponent in view while movement, jumps and attacks determine how to approach. Some Borgs specialise in close combat, others fire from a distance or support an ally. The collection matters because its members produce different tactical possibilities rather than simply another appearance.

cards.heading: The next Borg changes the battle
cards.text: When one Borg is defeated, the next member of the force enters and continues the battle. A good lineup therefore considers both individual strength and the order in which different abilities become available. Multiplayer lets players bring those decisions into matches with friends, while the campaign expands the roster through repeated encounters. Mitsuhiko Takano composed the music. The game's lasting appeal centres on this link between a crowded toy collection and the very specific fighting style of the next small character sent into the arena.

main.title: 1080° Avalanche
main.subtitle: Race down a mountain that will not stay still
main.summary: 1080° Avalanche is Nintendo Software Technology's snowboarding game, first released for GameCube in Europe on 28 November 2003.

cards.heading: Race down a mountain that will not stay still
cards.text: 1080° Avalanche is Nintendo Software Technology's snowboarding game, first released for GameCube in Europe on 28 November 2003. The sequel to 1080° Snowboarding emphasises downhill racing, asking the player to reach the finish ahead of a rival while reading the changing slope. Snow, obstacles and turns make the mountain itself part of the contest. Tricks remain available, but maintaining speed through a difficult section can matter more than taking the largest jump when another rider is already approaching the next turn.

cards.heading: Keep the board moving through the terrain
cards.text: The main Match Race mode sends the rider through successive challenges, while Time Trial, Trick Attack and Gate modes give the same control a different purpose. Each rider has individual boards to unlock, allowing the player to vary the equipment used for a run. Four-player split-screen makes the race a direct local contest, and LAN play supports connected GameCube systems. The different modes expose another side of a course, whether the immediate goal is a faster time, a clean route through gates or a higher trick score.

cards.heading: The avalanche follows the final run
cards.text: The final event in each Match Race challenge introduces the danger named in the title: an avalanche begins along the route and forces the rider to keep moving ahead of it. The familiar need to preserve speed becomes an urgent escape as the mountain breaks behind the board. Lawrence Schwedler and James Phillipsen composed the original score. These runs give the sequel its most distinctive image, turning the slope from a course to be mastered into a moving threat that follows the rider towards the finish.
